extraction.name: LUMA: A Benchmark Dataset for Leaming from Uncertain and Multimodal Data
extraction.description: We propose LUMA, a unique multimodal dataset, featuring audio, image, and textual data from 50 classes, specifically designed for leaming from uncertain data. It extends the well-known CIFAR 10/100 dataset with audio samples extracted from three audio corpora, and text data generated using the Gemma-7B Large Language Model (LLM). The LUMA dataset enables the controlled injection of varying types and degrees of uncertainty to achieve and tailor specific experiments and benchmarking initiatives. LUMA is also available as a Python package including the functions for generating multiple variants of the dataset with controlling the diversity of the data, the amount of noise for each modality, and adding out-of-distribution samples. A baseline pre-trained model is also provided alongside three uncertainty quantification methods: Monte-Carlo Dropout, Deep Ensemble, and Reliable Conflictive Multi-View Leaming. This comprehensive dataset and its tools are intended to promote and support the development, evaluation, and benchmarking of trustworthy and robust multimodal deep leaming approaches. We anticipate that the LUMA dataset will help the research community to design more trustworthy and robust machine leaming approaches for safety critical applications.

extraction.rai:dataCollection: LUMA is a multimodal dataset, featuring audio, image, and textual data from 50 classes. It includes 101,000 images, 135,096 speech audio recordings, and 62,875 text passages, amounting to approximately 3 GB of data. Each modality is independently sourced, reflecting real-world conditions where data is often collected under different conditions and times. The modalities are carefully aligned, ensuring that each text passage is related to the object in the corresponding image, and each audio recording is the pronunciation of the object label in the image. Images were compiled from the CIFAR 10/100 dataset. Audio samples corresponding to CIFAR image class labels were extracted, validated, and associated from three diverse audio corpora (The Spoken Wikipedia, LibriSpeech, and Mozilla Common Voice). Text modality was generated based on the class labels using the Gemma-7B Instruct Large Language Model (LLM). 73 additional recordings of pronunciations belonging to 4 classes were voluntarily contributed by colleagues, anonymized, trimmed, and added to the dataset.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator, Self-reporting
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images from the CIFAR 10/100 dataset. Audio samples from The Spoken Wikipedia [15], LibriSpeech [27], and Mozilla Common Voice [2] corpora. Text generated using Google’s Gemma-7B Instruct model [25]. 73 additional audio recordings voluntarily contributed by colleagues.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The provided Python toolkit allows the injection of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties in a controlled and parameterized way into each modality specifically. This includes controlling data diversity, adding different types of real-world noise, randomly switching labels to their closest class, and injecting out-of-distribution (OOD) data. For diversity control, deep features are extracted (Wav2Vec for audio, BERT for text, VGG-11 for images), and samples are drawn from a categorical distribution based on their inverse distance to the class center, raised to the power of k. For sample noise, background noise from ESC-50 dataset is added to audio, nlpaug library is used for text noise (keyboard, OCR, random character, antonym, random word, spelling, back-translation), and 15 perturbations (Gaussian, shot, impulse noise, various blurs, snow, frost, fog, brightness, contrast, elasticity, pixelating, JPEG compressing) are added to images. For label noise, a subset of samples has their labels altered by reassigning to the class with the lowest mean distance to its five nearest samples in deep feature space. OOD samples are taken from classes not present in the training data within the same dataset.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For the image modality, CIFAR-100 and CIFAR-10 datasets were chosen. 42 classes were selected to have at least 600 samples per class per modality after alignment. 8 classes with less than 600 samples were used as OOD samples. Images generated with EDM Diffusion-based generative model were included to alleviate the issue of having no more than 600 samples per class in CIFAR-100. For audio modality, audio segments corresponding to CIFAR-10/100 class labels (including plural forms) were extracted from The Spoken Wikipedia, LibriSpeech (using force-aligned alignments from Montreal Forced Aligner), and Mozilla Common Voice (using force-aligned alignments). Extracted audio samples were automatically validated using OpenAI’s Whisper Large V3 model for transcription; if transcription matched the label, it was considered valid. Samples not automatically validated were sent for manual validation. For text modality, Gemma-7B Instruct model was used to generate text segments about class labels using 13 different prompts. To validate, all label occurrences in the text were masked and fed back into the Gemma-7B Instruct model, asking it to classify the text into one of the labels; if the prediction matched the ground truth, the sample was accepted as validated.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Audio samples were automatically validated with OpenAI’s Whisper Large V3 model for transcription. If the transcription corresponded to the class label (or its plural form), the sample was considered valid. Otherwise, the sample was sent for manual validation. For manual validation, 8,372 samples from classes with less than 800 samples were scheduled. A labeling interface was built using Label Studio, providing the audio sample and the prompt 'Is the audio saying the word below? (An extra ’s’ or ’es’ in the pronunciation is okay.)' and answer options of 'Yes' or 'No'. 2 annotations per sample were collected from 17 annotators. Text samples were validated by masking all label occurrences in the generated text and feeding the masked text back into the Gemma-7B Instruct model, asking it to classify the text into one of the labels. If the prediction matched the ground truth label, the sample was accepted as validated.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: For manual audio validation, 71.61% annotation agreement was achieved. 5,027 samples where both annotators confirmed validity were accepted. Samples with conflicting annotations were rejected.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Our colleagues (M.Sc. and PhD students, and professors) with advanced to fluent English knowledge
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: OpenAI’s Whisper Large V3 model [29], Gemma-7B Instruct model [25]
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: We anticipate that the LUMA dataset will help the research community to design more trustworthy and robust machine leaming approaches for safety critical applications.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: After manually analyzing some of the generated texts, we noticed that there were samples with offensive biases and stereotypes, particularly gender bias for classes 'man', 'woman', 'boy' and 'girl'. Our hypothesis is, that describing a man or woman in an unbiased way is a challenging task for LLM models (as well as for humans), which are trained on unbalanced data [16]. Although the model identified a high level of bias in these classes, indicating a potential for LLM-based bias detection, we are unable to assess how accurate or consistent these detections truly are. To reduce the biases for these labels, prompts were reconstructed to explicitly provide topics and keywords with occupations, which minimized the bias, though a significant amount of bias still exists.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Since textual data was generated using an LLM, we recognize that the dataset may contain factual inaccuracies, or biases, but our aim is to offer a benchmark to study uncertainty quantification in multimodal classification settings. LUMA shall not be used as a source of knowledge or information. The performance of Monte Carlo Dropout and Deep Ensembles indicates a limitation in their suitability for OOD-detection in LUMA dataset. This suggests new avenues for further exploratory research to leverage uncertainty estimation for robust detection of out-of-distribution samples.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The LUMA dataset enables the controlled injection of varying types and degrees of uncertainty to achieve and tailor specific experiments and benchmarking initiatives. This comprehensive dataset and its tools are intended to promote and support the development, evaluation, and benchmarking of trustworthy and robust multimodal deep leaming approaches. It is specifically designed for benchmarking multimodal learning algorithms on uncertain data. The dataset can be used for training, testing, and validation of models, particularly for studying uncertainty quantification in multimodal classification settings and for OOD detection.
